clinicalPearls: This is an overgrowth-with-intellectual-disability syndrome characterised by tall stature, macrocephaly, and a recognisable facial appearance including a long, narrow face and prominent forehead

It is caused by variants in NFIX, a transcription factor gene; the overgrowth phenotype arises from a distinct molecular mechanism to that producing the separate, unrelated Marshall-Smith syndrome caused by other NFIX variants
Developmental delay and intellectual disability are typical, and behavioural features such as anxiety and autistic traits are common
A slender, marfanoid habitus with long limbs may prompt consideration of connective tissue disorders
Ophthalmological anomalies including strabismus and optic atrophy are recognised associations
Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genetic testing, often through genome or exome sequencing or a targeted overgrowth panel, having considered Sotos syndrome in the differential
There is no specific treatment; care is anticipatory and multidisciplinary, addressing development, behaviour, vision, and skeletal and cardiovascular surveillance as clinically indicated
reference.pathophysiology: Malan syndrome is a chromatin- and transcription-related overgrowth disorder caused by heterozygous variants in NFIX, which encodes a nuclear factor I transcription factor involved in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation during development, including in brain and skeletal tissue. Loss-of-function variants that reduce functional NFIX dosage disturb the tightly controlled transcriptional programmes governing growth, producing the characteristic tall stature, macrocephaly, and neurodevelopmental features. Notably, a separate class of NFIX variants causes the clinically distinct Marshall-Smith syndrome, illustrating how different molecular consequences at one locus generate divergent phenotypes. Most cases arise de novo and inheritance, when relevant, is autosomal dominant.
additionalDifferentials: Marfan syndrome and related connective tissue disorders
Other transcription- or chromatin-related overgrowth syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing, or a targeted overgrowth/intellectual disability gene panel
Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy number causes of overgrowth and developmental delay
MRI of the brain where neurological signs or macrocephaly warrant imaging
Ophthalmological assessment for strabismus and optic atrophy
Skeletal and cardiovascular assessment given the marfanoid habitus
redFlags: Rapidly increasing head circumference or neurological signs suggesting intracranial pathology
Features suggesting aortic root dilatation or other cardiovascular involvement in a marfanoid child
Significant regression of skills prompting re-evaluation
Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis relates chiefly to the degree of intellectual disability and any associated medical complications; lifespan is not clearly reduced in most individuals. Ongoing developmental, educational, and behavioural support improves function, and surveillance addresses ophthalmological and skeletal issues as they arise.
pitfalls: Confusing the disorder with Sotos syndrome and stopping testing at NSD1
Attributing the marfanoid habitus to a primary connective tissue disorder and missing the overgrowth syndrome
Overlooking anxiety and autistic features that benefit from targeted support
Assuming NFIX variants always cause the same phenotype, when they may instead cause Marshall-Smith syndrome
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: No disease-specific drug therapy exists; management is supportive with early developmental intervention including speech and language, occupational and physiotherapy and tailored educational support
Behavioural and psychological support for anxiety and autistic traits, with input from developmental paediatrics or psychiatry
Ophthalmological review and treatment of strabismus with surveillance for optic atrophy
Skeletal and cardiovascular assessment given the marfanoid habitus, with monitoring for related complications
Growth and head circumference monitoring coordinated by a multidisciplinary team including clinical genetics
Genetic counselling recognising autosomal dominant inheritance with most cases arising de novo, and confirmatory NFIX molecular testing
